d: Data type having a value of either true or false.
h:
The boolean data type, or bool, has a value of either true or false.

Conditionals

If a value isn't false or nil, Luau evaluates it as true in conditional statements. Unlike many other languages, Luau considers both zero and the empty string as true.

Operators

You can formulate complex conditions with relational and logical operators.

kid.simple: A boolean is a value that can only be `true` or `false`, like a light switch that is on or off. Games use booleans all the time, like `isAlive` or `doorIsOpen`. In `if` checks, Luau treats everything as true except `false` and `nil`. That means even `0` and empty text count as true.
kid.analogy: A boolean is a yes-or-no question. Is the door open? Yes (`true`) or no (`false`). There is no "maybe".
keyPoints: The boolean type, also called `bool`, has only two values: `true` and `false`.
In an `if` statement, only `false` and `nil` count as false.
Unlike many other languages, `0` and the empty string `""` count as true in Luau.
You can build bigger conditions with comparison operators like `==`, `<`, `>` and logic operators like `and`, `or`, `not`.
Comparisons give back booleans. For example, `5 > 3` is `true`.

terms.boolean: A value that is either `true` or `false`.
terms.conditional statement: Code that only runs if something is true, like `if isAlive then ... end`.
terms.evaluate: To work out what a value counts as. `if 0 then` evaluates `0` as true.
terms.relational operator: A comparison like `==`, `~=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`. It gives `true` or `false`.
terms.logical operator: `and`, `or`, `not`. They combine or flip true/false checks.
terms.empty string: Text with nothing in it, written `""`.

example.title: Open a door only if the player has a key
example.code:
local hasKey = true
local doorIsLocked = true

if hasKey and doorIsLocked then
	doorIsLocked = false
	print("Door unlocked!")
end

print("Is the door locked?", doorIsLocked) --> false

-- 0 and "" count as true in Luau
if 0 then
	print("0 counts as true")
end
explain: `and` means both must be true for the code inside to run.
Inside, the door is unlocked by setting `doorIsLocked` to `false`.
The last `if` shows that `0` counts as true in Luau.

watchOut: Writing `if coins then` to check for zero coins. `0` is true in Luau, so write `if coins > 0 then`.
Writing the string `"false"` instead of the boolean `false`. Any string, even "false", counts as true.
Using `=` instead of `==` in a check. `=` sets a value; `==` compares.
